justice: The street allocates substantial space to multiple modes, with a motor-vehicle carriageway on the left and a separately paved side path on the right, suggesting some distribution of space beyond cars only.

A continuous metal barrier divides the main roadway from the side path, which helps organize movement but may also limit flexible crossing opportunities and reduce equal convenience between both sides of the corridor.

The right-side path is wide and mostly flat, which supports access for many users, but no visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossings can be identified in this view, weakening fully inclusive accessibility.
Street lighting is provided on both sides through tall lamp posts, indicating some even provision of public infrastructure along the corridor.
safety: The long central metal guardrail creates clear separation between the motor lane and the adjacent side path, reducing direct conflict between faster vehicles and slower users.
The roadway is wide and visually open, giving drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians long sightlines ahead, which generally improves reaction time.
Dedicated streetlights are present along the corridor, supporting basic nighttime safety infrastructure even though daylight conditions prevent judging illumination quality.
No visible marked pedestrian crossing, refuge island, or traffic-calming feature appears in the image, so crossing the corridor may still be difficult and potentially unsafe.
livability: The dense row of mature trees on the right provides a greener edge and makes the corridor feel less harsh than a fully paved industrial street.
The left side contains long blank-fronted building facades and utility poles rather than active storefronts or seating, which limits street life and social interaction.
Very few people are visible in the scene, and there are no obvious public gathering amenities such as benches, bus shelters, or small plazas, reducing everyday social vibrancy.
The street appears clean and orderly, with maintained planting beds and a tidy paved surface, which supports basic environmental quality.
sustainability: The large tree canopy on the right contributes to urban cooling, shade, and ecological value compared with a fully exposed corridor.
The separated side path can support low-carbon travel such as cycling and walking, reducing dependence on private motor vehicles.
A drainage channel is visible along the left curb, indicating stormwater management infrastructure, although no clear permeable bioswale or rain garden is visible.
Overhead utility lines and extensive hard paving remain prominent, so the corridor still relies heavily on grey infrastructure rather than fully integrated green infrastructure.
aesthetics: The continuous line of mature trees on the right creates a strong green visual frame and improves scenic quality.
The streetlights have a consistent, decorative curved form, adding visual order and design coherence to the corridor.
The road and side path look relatively clean and uncluttered, which strengthens the overall impression of maintenance.
Visual quality is somewhat reduced by the heavy bundle of overhead utility wires and the plain industrial-style building frontage on the left.
comfort: Thermal comfort is mixed: the right side benefits from significant shade from mature trees, while the main roadway and left-side edge are largely exposed to direct sun.
The right-side path appears wide, smooth, and mostly level, which supports comfortable movement for walking and cycling.
There are no visible benches, resting places, or shelters along the corridor, reducing physical comfort for users who need pauses or weather protection.
Psychological comfort benefits from the open sightlines and low apparent congestion, but the long barrier and broad road width can make the environment feel somewhat austere and vehicle-oriented.
walkability: A wide side path exists on the right and appears continuous in this view, providing space for pedestrians away from moving traffic.
The metal barrier separates pedestrians from the main carriageway, which improves protection but may also make route access and crossing less convenient.
No visible zebra crossing, curb ramp, pedestrian signal, or tactile guidance is present in the image, limiting confidence in complete pedestrian connectivity.
Shade from the tree line improves walking conditions on one side, but the corridor overall feels oriented toward through movement rather than active pedestrian destinations.
bikeability: The broad separated side path on the right appears suitable for cycling and offers better protection than mixing directly with motor traffic.
The central barrier reduces direct encroachment from vehicles into the adjacent non-motorized space, which improves perceived cycling safety.
The corridor is flat, straight, and has long visibility, all of which support easy bicycle travel.
No clear bicycle symbols, colored lane markings, or visible bicycle parking are present, so cycling support is functional but not fully legible or fully equipped.
